definition: Binding precedent is a legal rule or principle, articulated by an appellate court, that must be followed by lower courts within its jurisdiction. Essentially, once an appellate court reviews a case, it will deliver a written opinion. This written opinion will include the court’s determination on a question of law. This determination, known as a holding, is binding on all lower courts within the jurisdiction, meaning that lower courts must apply this decision when presented with similar facts. The lower courts are thus bound, or required to follow the legal precedent set by the higher court. The Supreme Court, for example, is the highest court in the U.S., and so, its decisions are binding on all other courts in the U.S. Alternatively, the decisions of the highest court in New York are only binding on other New York courts, but not courts in other states.
